_meta.purpose: Two intertwined family trees of Bharat, kept deliberately separate: (1) the LANGUAGE tree — which language descends from which, grouped by family (Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austroasiatic, Tibeto-Burman); and (2) the SCRIPT tree — which alphabet descends from which, almost all rooted in ancient Brahmi. The point the whole page makes: India's languages come from unrelated families (Tamil is NOT from Sanskrit), yet nearly all of their SCRIPTS share ONE ancestor — Brahmi. The languages diverge; the writing systems converge. That convergence is the entire premise of the modern 'Bharati' link-script (IIT Madras).
_meta.honesty: We keep three things strictly apart, because people constantly blur them: (a) a LANGUAGE and (b) the SCRIPT it happens to be written in are two different inheritance trees — Sanskrit was written in many scripts before Devanagari; (c) an ESTABLISHED fact (Brahmi is attested 3rd c. BCE; Tamil is Dravidian) versus a CONTESTED interpretation (where Brahmi itself came from; whether a constructed link-script is desirable). Brahmi's own parentage is genuinely disputed and we flag it, not resolve it. Dead languages/scripts are labelled as such.
the_two_truths: Tamil (Dravidian) and Sanskrit (Indo-European/Indo-Aryan) belong to UNRELATED language families — different roots, different grammar. Tamil is NOT descended from Sanskrit.
Yet the Tamil script and Devanagari BOTH descend from Brahmi. Unrelated languages, one shared script-ancestor. This is why one neutral 'link script' (Bharati) is even structurally conceivable.

key_terms.abugida: A writing system where each consonant carries an inherent vowel (usually 'a'), and other vowels are shown by attached marks. Brahmi and ALL its descendants — and Bharati — are abugidas. This shared structure is what makes a common script possible across families.
key_terms.language_family: A group of languages descended from one common ancestral language. India spans several UNRELATED families; that they share script-ancestry is a separate fact from language descent.
key_terms.dead_language: A language with no living native-speaker community. It may still be used liturgically/academically (Sanskrit, Pali, Latin) or be wholly extinct (Tocharian).
key_terms.link_script / bridge script: One neutral script used to write many languages, the way the Latin alphabet writes English, Spanish, Turkish, Vietnamese… 'Bharati' proposes this for India.

sources.label: Brahmi script — Wikipedia (origins, Ashokan attestation, parent/child/sister systems, Prinsep decipherment)
Bharati script — Wikipedia (IIT Madras link-script, V. Srinivasa Chakravarthy)
Brahmic scripts — Wikipedia (the full Brahmic family, Northern & Southern branches)
Salomon, R. (1998), 'Indian Epigraphy', Oxford University Press

specimen.purpose: Seeing is believing: the SAME Sanskrit word — saṃskṛtam, 'refined / put-together', the name of the language itself — written across many scripts. Sanskrit has no script of its own; it borrows whichever local Brahmic script is at hand. That the same sounds render in utterly different-looking letters is the visible proof that LANGUAGE and SCRIPT are separate trees. Rendered with your device's Unicode fonts; a script may show boxes if the font is missing.
specimen.word_meaning: saṃskṛtam — 'refined, perfected, put-together' — the endonym of the Sanskrit language.

renderings.caveat: Tamil script lacks distinct letters for several Sanskrit sounds (no aspirates, one 's'), so this is an approximation — the very gap Grantha was invented to fill.

renderings.script: Grantha (built to write Sanskrit in the south)
renderings.caveat: Grantha is an astral-plane Unicode block; if your device lacks a Grantha font this line shows boxes — itself a small demonstration that a script needs its font to be 'alive' on a screen.

renderings.script: Brahmi (the ancient root — a dead script)
renderings.caveat: Classical Sanskrit postdates the Ashokan Brahmi corpus (which is in Prakrit); this is a modern Brahmi-Unicode transcription of the sounds, shown to place the root — not a genuine ancient attestation. Rendered with a bundled Noto Sans Brahmi font.

origins.title: Where did Brahmi come from? — the honest, unresolved answer
origins.standfirst: Brahmi appears in the record already fully formed, in Ashoka's edicts of the 3rd century BCE. Where it came from before that is one of the genuinely OPEN questions of Indian history — and a politically charged one. Here are the live theories, kept as theories.
origins.the_gap: The core difficulty: there is no clear evidence of writing in the subcontinent for roughly 1,500 years between the collapse of the Indus Valley Civilisation (~1900 BCE) and the first securely dated Brahmi (~3rd century BCE). That silent gap is what every theory has to explain — and why none is conclusively proven.

theories.name: Semitic / Aramaic derivation
theories.proponents: Albrecht Weber (1856), Georg Bühler (1895); reviewed by Salomon (1998), Falk (1993)
theories.claim: Brahmi was adapted from a Semitic script — most often the Aramaic (or Phoenician) alphabet — reaching India through trade contacts, then heavily reworked to fit Indian phonology and turned into an abugida.
theories.for: Aramaic was a real administrative script on India's northwest frontier; some letter-shapes and the general alphabetic idea can be lined up. It is the mainstream scholarly position.
theories.against: The match is loose and much had to be invented (the systematic vowel-marking, the ordering by phonetics). 'The issue is not settled due to the lack of direct evidence.'

theories.name: Indigenous / Indus-script origin
theories.stance: held by a number of (often Indian) scholars
theories.proponents: various; a recurring position among Indian epigraphists
theories.claim: Brahmi developed within India, possibly evolving from or inspired by the earlier Indus (Harappan) script — an unbroken indigenous tradition of writing.
theories.for: Brahmi is beautifully fitted to Indian sounds, as a home-grown system would be; avoids assuming everything came from outside.
theories.against: The Indus script is UNDECIPHERED and separated from Brahmi by the ~1,500-year gap with no attested writing in between — so the bridge is asserted, not demonstrated. Remains inconclusive.

theories.name: Pictographic-acrophonic origin
theories.claim: Brahmi letters began as little pictures, each standing for the first sound of the pictured word (acrophony), then abstracted into letters.
theories.for: A tidy story of how any script might begin from drawings.
theories.against: Not supported by evidence and no longer widely accepted; included to show how theories rise and fall.

origins.politics: Salomon and others note this debate carries baggage: the Semitic-origin view has been criticised as reflecting a colonial-era 'imperialist bias' (nothing important could be purely Indian), while the indigenous view can carry a 'nationalist bias' (everything important must be purely Indian). We report the theories and their evidence, and let the gap stand where the gap is.
origins.decipherment: None of this was even readable until 1837, when James Prinsep of the Asiatic Society of Bengal cracked Brahmi (and soon Kharoshthi), with Alexander Cunningham's help — using, among other clues, bilingual Indo-Greek coins. At a stroke, Ashoka's edicts and centuries of Indian inscriptions became legible again. The origin of Brahmi is unsettled; the moment we regained the ABILITY TO READ it is precisely dated.
origins.verdict: Established: Brahmi is attested from the 3rd c. BCE and is an abugida, root of ~198 later scripts. Unresolved: where it ultimately came from. We hold that line honestly — the same discipline as the Aryan-migration question on the DNA page.

analysis.title: How a script works — and why unrelated languages ended up sharing one
analysis.standfirst: A language is a system of sound and meaning; a script is only the clothing we put on it to make it visible. Confusing the two is the single most common mistake in these debates. Here is the mechanism, step by step.

p: A language is spoken first and can exist with no writing at all — most human languages never had a script. A script is a technology bolted on later to record it. The proof is everywhere in India: Sanskrit was transmitted orally for a thousand years before it touched a pen, and even then it was written in Brahmi, then Gupta, then Grantha in the south and Sharada in Kashmir, and only much later settled on Devanagari. One language, many scripts. Conversely one script can carry many languages — Devanagari today writes Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, Konkani and Sanskrit, which are not the same language.
So a language has a family tree (who it descended from) and, separately, a script history (which alphabets have been used to write it). These two trees run on different clocks and must be read apart.

Brahmi and all its children are abugidas — halfway between an alphabet (where every vowel is a full letter, as in Latin) and a syllabary (where each symbol is a whole syllable). In an abugida, a consonant letter carries a built-in inherent vowel, usually short 'a'. So the bare letter क is already 'ka', not just 'k'. To write a different vowel you attach a mark: का 'kā', कि 'ki', कु 'ku'. To kill the vowel entirely you add a virama/halant stroke: क् is a bare 'k'.

This one design choice is why the whole family feels related even when the letters look nothing alike. Tamil க, Telugu క, Bengali ক, Malayalam ക and Devanagari क are visually unrelated — but they all mean the same thing: the consonant 'k' plus an inherent 'a', modified by attached vowel-marks. Same underlying logic, different surface. That shared logic is the hinge on which a single link-script can turn.
Brahmi diversified for three concrete reasons, and you can still see each one in the letters today.

The writing surface. Much of India wrote on palm leaf with a stylus. A straight horizontal stroke would split the leaf along its fibres, so southern and eastern scripts rounded their letters — this is why Telugu, Kannada, Odia, Sinhala and the Southeast-Asian scripts are so curvy, while the north, writing more on birch-bark and paper, kept angular forms and even added the shirorekha, the horizontal headline bar you see across the top of Devanagari and Bengali words.

New sounds. When Brahmi met a language with sounds it lacked, letters were invented or dropped. Tamil-Brahmi shed the aspirates and extra sibilants Tamil never used, and added Dravidian sounds like ழ. In the far south, because the Tamil script could not fully spell Sanskrit, a separate script — Grantha — was created just for it, and Grantha in turn seeded the Malayalam script. Adaptation to phonology is the main engine of divergence.

Time and prestige. Empires and religions carried scripts far and re-cut them in local taste: Pallava traders and Buddhist and Hindu missionaries exported Brahmic writing across Southeast Asia, where it became Khmer, Thai, Burmese, Balinese and more. One survey counts 198 scripts ultimately descended from Brahmi — one of the most prolific writing traditions on Earth.

sections.h: 4 · Why unrelated languages share a script
p: Here is the crux. Dravidian (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam) and Indo-Aryan (Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, and their ancestor Sanskrit) are genuinely unrelated language families — different roots, different grammar; Tamil is not descended from Sanskrit. Yet Tamil and Hindi are both written in Brahmi-descended scripts. Why?

Because a script spreads by contact and prestige, not by descent. When the Mauryan state and the Buddhist and Jain and Brahmanical traditions carried literacy south and east, the peoples there adopted the writing technology — Brahmi's abugida — and fitted it to their own, unrelated speech. The languages stayed foreign to each other; the writing system was shared, then localised. This is exactly how the Latin alphabet came to write English, Turkish, Vietnamese and Swahili — languages from four different families — none of which descend from Latin.

So the map of scripts is a map of cultural contact, laid over a map of languages that is a record of descent. They rhyme in places and diverge in others, and reading them together is how you separate 'who influenced whom' from 'who came from whom'.

Because every Indian script shares Brahmi's abugida structure, it is technically possible to design one neutral script that writes all of them — mapping the same consonant-plus-vowel-mark logic onto a single new set of shapes. That is precisely what Bharati (IIT Madras) attempts, borrowing strokes from several scripts and dropping the headline bar for a cleaner line, so a Tamil and a Hindi speaker could read each other's languages in one common alphabet — the way Europeans read each other in Latin letters.

But a script is never only a technology. It is identity. Tamil's distinct script is bound up with a proud history of resisting Sanskrit and Hindi imposition; a single national script reads to many as erasure, not convenience. This is why the honest verdict on Bharati is split: structurally elegant, politically fraught, and — unlike ancient dead Brahmi — not even in Unicode yet. The engineering is the easy part; the meaning people attach to their letters is the hard part.

edict.purpose: A ruler's own words, in stone, ~2,270 years old. Ashoka's Major Rock Edict 13 is where he records the Kalinga war and — extraordinarily for a conqueror — his remorse. This is why the script matters: because Brahmi was deciphered, we can VERIFY what a Mauryan emperor actually proclaimed and what his rule was like, from his commissioned text rather than from later legend.
edict.title: Ashoka — Major Rock Edict 13 (on the Kalinga war)
edict.when: war c. 261–260 BCE (8th year of Ashoka's reign); edict carved c. 250 BCE
edict.script: Brahmi (Kharoshthi in the northwest; Greek & Aramaic on the frontier)
english: When King Beloved-of-the-Gods, Priyadarsin, had been anointed eight years, (the country of) the Kalingas was conquered by (him). One hundred and fifty thousand in number were the men who were deported thence, one hundred thousand in number were those who were slain there, and many times as many those who died.

After that, now that (the country of) the Kalingas has been taken, Beloved-of-the-Gods (is devoted) to a zealous study of morality (Dharma), to the love of morality, and to the instruction (of people) in morality. This is the repentance of Beloved-of-the-Gods on account of his conquest of (the country of) the Kalingas.

brahmi_phrase.caveat: A modern Brahmi-Unicode transcription of Ashoka's title Devānaṃpiya ('Beloved-of-the-Gods'), the epithet by which the edicts name him — shown so you can read a fragment of the actual script. It is a transcription for legibility, NOT a facsimile of any one stone; carved letter-forms vary by site. Rendered with a bundled Noto Sans Brahmi font.

edict.how_we_know: The edicts were unreadable for ~2,000 years until James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837–38 (with Alexander Cunningham). This translation is E. Hultzsch's, from 'Inscriptions of Asoka' (1925, public domain). Because the same edict survives at many sites — Kalsi, Girnar, Shahbazgarhi, Dhauli and more — we can cross-check the text and map where Mauryan authority reached.

source.label: Ashoka, Major Rock Edict 13; trans. E. Hultzsch, 'Inscriptions of Asoka' (1925)

earliest_scripts.purpose: What writing looked like in the Mauryan era (c. 322–185 BCE) and before — the primary evidence for how things actually were. Ashoka's edicts are the point where a RULER'S OWN WORDS survive in stone: what he claimed, the ethics (dhamma) he proclaimed, and how far his writ ran (the edicts' spread maps the empire). To read the Maurya on their own terms rather than through later retellings, you read Brahmi.
earliest_scripts.ashoka_note: The Edicts of Ashoka (c. 268–232 BCE) are among the world's oldest surviving royal proclamations — carved on pillars and rocks across the empire, mostly in Prakrit written in Brahmi (and in Kharoshthi in the northwest, Greek & Aramaic on the frontier). They are how we VERIFY what Ashoka said and what his rule was like — remorse after the Kalinga war, welfare works, religious tolerance, the spread of dhamma — from his own commissioned text, not hearsay. Their find-spots trace the reach of Mauryan authority.

items.name: Indus (Harappan) script
items.note: Short seal-inscriptions of the Indus Valley Civilisation, ~1500 years before the Maurya. UNDECIPHERED — we cannot read a single sentence, nor confirm it is full writing. So for the deep past we have material remains but no readable words: history without a legible voice.

items.name: Megalithic / South Indian graffiti symbols
items.note: Non-verbal or proto-writing marks on megalithic pottery. Some scholars see a bridge toward Tamil-Brahmi; unproven. Included honestly as a debated, mostly-unread symbol system, not established writing.

items.name: Brahmi
items.note: The script of the Mauryan state. Fully formed in Ashoka's edicts (c. 250 BCE) — the earliest large body of READABLE Indian text, and the primary record of what a ruler proclaimed. Deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837, which reopened the entire early history of India to reading. Root of ~198 later scripts. Its own parentage is contested.

items.name: Tamil-Brahmi
items.note: A southern adaptation of Brahmi, adding letters for Tamil (Dravidian) sounds Brahmi lacked. Cave inscriptions in Tamil Nadu. Shows the Mauryan-era script reaching the Dravidian south and being re-tooled for a different language family.

items.name: Kharoshthi
items.note: The other Mauryan-era script — used in the northwest, derived from Aramaic, written right-to-left. Some Ashokan edicts on the frontier are in Kharoshthi (and even Greek & Aramaic), showing the multilingual edge of the empire. A dead end: it left no living descendants and vanished by the 3rd c. CE.

families.label: Indo-Aryan
families.note: A branch of Indo-European — kin to Persian, Greek, Latin, Slavic, English. Entered South Asia with the Steppe/Indo-Iranian expansion (see the DNA record). Sanskrit is its classical ancestor.

families.label: Dravidian
families.note: An indigenous South Asian family with NO established relation to Indo-European. Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam. Tamil is NOT derived from Sanskrit.

families.label: Austroasiatic
families.note: Munda (Santali, Ho, Mundari) in central/east India + Khasi in the northeast; kin to Khmer and Vietnamese far to the east. Some tribal languages here had NO script until modern times.

families.label: Tibeto-Burman
families.note: Sino-Tibetan branch of the northeast and Himalaya: Meitei (Manipuri), Bodo, Mizo, and many others.

families.label: Constructed
families.note: Not a natural family — an invented system. Bharati script is here: a designed abugida, not a descendant of any one script.

languages.name: Proto-Dravidian
languages.note: The unattested common ancestor of all Dravidian languages, reconstructed by comparison — never written down. Argued by many scholars to predate Indo-Aryan arrival in the subcontinent.

languages.name: Old Tamil
languages.note: The language of the Sangam corpus — some of the oldest secular literature in India. First written in Tamil-Brahmi. This is the deep root of living Tamil.

languages.name: Tamil (modern)
languages.note: A LIVING Dravidian language, directly descended from Old Tamil — NOT from Sanskrit. Its distinctness from Sanskrit/Hindi is central to Tamil identity and to the politics that make an imposed common script sensitive.

languages.name: Telugu
languages.note: Dravidian, but heavily Sanskrit-influenced in vocabulary (a loan relationship, NOT descent). Written in the Telugu script (Brahmi-descended, close cousin of Kannada).

languages.name: Kannada
languages.note: Dravidian; its script and Telugu's split from one common Kadamba/Old-Kannada ancestor.

languages.name: Malayalam
languages.note: The youngest major Dravidian language — diverged from Old/Middle Tamil ~9th c. CE. Its script grew out of Grantha (used for Sanskrit) + Vaṭṭeḻuttu.

languages.name: Proto-Indo-European (PIE)
languages.note: The unattested common ancestor of Indo-European — the ultimate source of Sanskrit AND of Latin, Greek, Persian, English. Associated with the Steppe/Yamnaya expansion in the DNA record.

languages.name: Proto-Indo-Iranian
languages.note: The branch of PIE ancestral to both the Iranian languages (Avestan, Persian) and the Indo-Aryan languages (Sanskrit onward).

languages.name: Vedic Sanskrit
languages.note: The language of the Vedas — transmitted ORALLY for centuries before it was ever written; only later committed to Brahmi and its descendants. This is why Sanskrit is 'script-agnostic'.

languages.name: Classical Sanskrit
languages.note: A DEAD language in the technical sense — no native-speaker community — surviving as a liturgical, scholarly and classical language (like Latin). Crucially it was NOT tied to Devanagari: it was written in whatever local Brahmic script was at hand (Grantha in the south, Sharada in Kashmir…). Devanagari became its default only later.

languages.name: Prakrits
languages.note: The everyday spoken Indo-Aryan vernaculars that stood beside formal Sanskrit — the actual bridge to the modern languages. Ashoka's edicts are in Prakrit, written in Brahmi (and Kharoshthi in the northwest). Now dead.

languages.name: Pali
languages.note: A Middle Indo-Aryan (Prakritic) language — the canonical language of Theravada Buddhism. Dead as a mother tongue but alive liturgically across South & Southeast Asia; written in whichever local Brahmic script the Buddhist community uses.

languages.name: Hindi
languages.period: living · largest by speakers in India
languages.note: A living Indo-Aryan language (via Apabhramsha from the Prakrits, i.e. ultimately the Sanskritic line). Written in Devanagari. The push to make Hindi/Devanagari a national link is precisely what Dravidian-speaking states resist.

languages.name: Bengali
languages.note: Indo-Aryan (Eastern), via the Prakrit → Apabhramsha line. Written in the Bengali–Assamese script.

languages.name: Marathi
languages.note: Indo-Aryan (Southern), from Maharashtri Prakrit. Written in Devanagari (historically also Modi).

languages.name: Santali
languages.note: A Munda (Austroasiatic) language — a DIFFERENT family again. For most of its history it had NO script of its own; the purpose-built Ol Chiki script (1925) and, before that, Bengali/Devanagari were used. Exactly the 'tribal language lacking a script' case a link-script aims at.

languages.name: Meitei (Manipuri)
languages.note: A Tibeto-Burman (Sino-Tibetan) language of Manipur — yet another family. Its own Meitei Mayek script was revived after centuries of being written in the Bengali–Assamese script.

languages.name: Tocharian
languages.note: A wholly EXTINCT Indo-European language of the Tarim Basin (NW China) — a striking case: an Indo-European language written in a Brahmi-derived script, far outside India. Listed among Brahmi's languages on the infobox.

languages.name: Indus Valley language(s)
languages.note: UNKNOWN and UNDECIPHERED. The Indus (Harappan) script has never been read, so we cannot even name the language family. Some argue it seeded Brahmi (indigenous-origin theory); a ~1500-year gap with no writing makes this contested. Kept explicitly as an open question, not an answer.

scripts.name: Indus (Harappan) script
scripts.note: The seals of the Indus Valley Civilisation. NEVER deciphered; we don't know if it's even full writing. A minority theory makes it Brahmi's ancestor (the 'indigenous origin' view) — unproven, and separated from Brahmi by ~1500 years with no attested writing in between.

scripts.name: Brahmi
scripts.decipherment: Deciphered by James Prinsep, 1837 (Asiatic Society of Bengal).
scripts.attestation: Fully formed in the Edicts of Ashoka, e.g. the Ashoka Pillar at Sarnath, c. 250 BCE.
scripts.note: THE ROOT of nearly every Indian script (and ~198 scripts across South & SE Asia). An abugida — consonant + inherent vowel — the structural pattern every descendant inherits. Now a DEAD script (nobody writes Brahmi today) though it IS in Unicode. Its own PARENT is genuinely disputed: the dominant Western view derives it from the Semitic/Aramaic alphabet (Weber 1856, Bühler 1895); an indigenous view ties it to the Indus script; both remain debated. We flag the parentage, we do not resolve it.

scripts.name: Kharoshthi
scripts.note: A SIBLING of Brahmi, not a child — the other ancient script of the subcontinent, used in the northwest (Gandhara). Written right-to-left, derived from Aramaic. Left NO living descendants and died out by the 3rd c. CE. A dead branch of the tree.

scripts.name: Gupta (Late Brahmi)
scripts.note: The transitional 'Late Brahmi' of the Gupta empire — the hinge from which the Northern scripts (Nagari → Devanagari, Sharada, Siddham) fan out. Dead itself, but the direct ancestor of Devanagari.

scripts.name: Nāgarī
scripts.note: The medieval script between Gupta and modern Devanagari.

scripts.name: Devanagari
scripts.note: The most-used Brahmic script today — Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, and the default modern script for Sanskrit. Note the headline (shirorekha) bar across the top of letters, which Bharati deliberately drops. Indo-Aryan side of the tree.

scripts.name: Sharada
scripts.note: The old script of Kashmir, once used for Sanskrit and Kashmiri; now nearly dead, surviving mainly in ritual use. Ancestor of Gurmukhi via the Landa scripts.

scripts.name: Gurmukhi
scripts.note: The script of Punjabi (Indo-Aryan), standardised for the Sikh scriptures. Descends from the Sharada/Landa line.

scripts.name: Bengali–Assamese
scripts.note: Writes Bengali, Assamese, and (historically) Meitei. Like Devanagari it keeps a headline bar. Eastern Indo-Aryan side.

scripts.name: Odia
scripts.note: Its distinctive curved letters come from writing on palm leaves (straight strokes would split the leaf). Indo-Aryan.

scripts.name: Gujarati
scripts.note: A Nagari-derived script that DROPS the top headline bar — the same feature Bharati borrows for a cleaner, more Latin-like line.

scripts.name: Meitei Mayek
scripts.note: The indigenous script of Meitei (Tibeto-Burman), revived after centuries of the language being written in Bengali–Assamese.

scripts.name: Tamil-Brahmi
scripts.note: The southern adaptation of Brahmi that first wrote Old Tamil — the start of the Dravidian side of the SCRIPT tree (the LANGUAGE stays Dravidian throughout).

scripts.name: Vaṭṭeḻuttu
scripts.note: 'Rounded script' — the medieval Tamil/Malabar script between Tamil-Brahmi and the modern Tamil script.

scripts.name: Tamil (modern script)
scripts.note: The living Tamil script — Brahmi-descended like Devanagari, even though the Tamil LANGUAGE is Dravidian and unrelated to Sanskrit. This split (shared script-ancestor, unrelated languages) is the whole story.

scripts.name: Grantha
scripts.note: The southern script used to write SANSKRIT (which Tamil script could not fully represent). Grantha is the bridge that seeded the Malayalam script — a neat proof that Sanskrit rode on many scripts. Now nearly dead.

scripts.name: Telugu
scripts.note: Telugu and Kannada scripts split from one common Kadamba ancestor; rounded forms, no headline bar. Dravidian language.

scripts.name: Kannada
scripts.note: Sister script to Telugu from the Kadamba/Old-Kannada line. Dravidian language.

scripts.name: Malayalam
scripts.note: Grew from Grantha (+ Vaṭṭeḻuttu) — so a Dravidian language written in a script that came partly through the Sanskrit-writing Grantha line. The trees cross here.

scripts.name: Sinhala
scripts.note: Sri Lanka. Writes Sinhala (Indo-Aryan!) and, liturgically, Pali — an Indo-Aryan language in a Southern-branch script, showing the script/language trees are independent.

scripts.name: Burmese
scripts.note: Beyond India: Brahmi (via Pallava/Mon) seeded the scripts of Burma, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, Bali and the Philippines — ~198 scripts in all. Rounded to suit palm-leaf writing.

scripts.name: Thai
scripts.note: Via Khmer ← Pallava ← Brahmi. Writes Thai and, liturgically, Pali. The Brahmic family reaches the whole of mainland Southeast Asia.

scripts.name: Ol Chiki
scripts.note: A PURPOSE-BUILT script (Raghunath Murmu, 1925) created to give Santali (Austroasiatic) its own writing — NOT Brahmi-derived. The direct precedent for the idea of deliberately designing a script for a language that lacked one — which is what Bharati does, but for all of them at once.

scripts.name: Bharati
scripts.creator: V. Srinivasa Chakravarthy & team, IIT Madras
scripts.note: A CONSTRUCTED link-script — one neutral abugida meant to write ALL of India's 22 scheduled languages, across BOTH the Indo-Aryan and Dravidian families, the way the Latin alphabet serves Europe. It borrows glyph elements from Devanagari, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Bengali–Assamese and Latin, and drops the top headline bar (like Gujarati). It is NOT descended from Brahmi — it is designed — but it only works BECAUSE all those scripts share Brahmi's abugida structure. Status: a proposal, NOT adopted into Unicode — so unlike ancient dead Brahmi, this modern script has no code block yet. Whether such a link-script is desirable is genuinely contested (Tamil script-pride and anti-imposition politics in particular).
